query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the fraction of oxygen-affinity elements (e.g., Cr or Al) in high-entropy alloy protective coatings promotes the rapid formation of a stable, adherent oxide tribo-layer during wear, which significantly reduces wear rates compared to coatings with lower oxygen-affinity element content.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy coatings with conventional, baseline amounts of oxygen-affinity elements (e.g., Cr, Al) fabricated via standard processing methods.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the composition fraction of oxygen-affinity elements (e.g., adjust Cr and/or Al content) in the HEA coating.
generation.conditions: Controlled pin‐on‐disk wear testing under moderate to high sliding loads and speeds in oxygen-rich ambient or a controlled oxygenated atmosphere, with in-situ surface characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS/XPS).
generation.structural_mediator: The in-situ formed protective oxide tribo-layer that develops on the coating surface during wear.
generation.mechanism: The higher concentration of oxygen-affinity elements enhances the rapid formation and adherence of a protective oxide layer during sliding. This layer acts as a barrier that prevents direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby reducing wear and friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with increased oxygen-affinity element content will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced friction coefficients, attributable to a more uniform and adherent oxide tribo-layer, compared to baseline coatings.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings with standard oxygen-affinity element proportions under identical wear testing conditions.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to hold under moderate to high wear loads in oxygen-rich environments; under extreme conditions (e.g., very high loads or temperatures), the oxide layer may spall or deteriorate, potentially diminishing the observed benefit.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of oxygen-affinity element concentration required for optimal oxide layer formation and long-term durability of the protective film under cyclic or variable wear conditions is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one with a baseline composition and one with an increased fraction of oxygen-affinity elements (Cr/Al). Subject both sets to identical pin‐on‐disk wear tests under controlled moderate-to-high loads and in an oxygen-rich atmosphere. Use in-situ SEM/EDS/XPS to monitor oxide formation during wear.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss or wear volume)
Surface oxide layer thickness, uniformity, and composition (via SEM/EDS/XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with higher oxygen-affinity element content do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and friction coefficient, or if the protective oxide layer does not exhibit improved uniformity or adherence compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. chosen.conditions: A series of high-entropy alloy coatings with systematically varied oxygen-affinity element content are tested under controlled wear conditions (varying loads and sliding speeds from moderate to high) in oxygen-rich ambient environments
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the open question by testing the mechanistic hypothesis that wear resistance is governed by the in-situ formation of a protective oxide tribo‐layer whose quality is controlled by the alloy’s oxygen-affinity element content. It distinguishes the hypothesis from the baseline by employing a controlled compositional change and observing the correlated improvements (or lack thereof) in wear performance, using standard, well‐established techniques in the field.
